papers.full_text: nature health News ‘Desperate rodents’ pose hantavirus risk to humans — boosted by climate change and deforestation Rapid urbanization and changes in rodent behaviour increase the risk of human disease outbreaks, especially in Africa, but experts fear surveillance gaps leave most zoonotic infections undetected. By Tsitsi Bhobo W hen the Andes hantavirus cir­ culated on the M/V Hondius cruise ship, South Africa’s specialist hospitals quickly admitted infected patients and sequenced the virus. But infectious dis­ ease scientists warn that locally derived hanta­ virus strains — including the lethal Sangassou virus — are circulating undetected, hosted by native shrews, rodents and bats1. “At the moment, we believe that hanta­ virus probably is more prevalent [and] widespread than diagnosed in Africa,” says Tulio de Oliveira, Professor at Stellenbosch University, South Africa, and director of the Centre for Epidemic Response and Innova­ tion. Such infections are mainly “self-limited transmission clusters between rodents, other animals and humans,” he tells Nature Health. De Oliveira’s lab is one of a small number across Africa that test for viruses in wild animals, including rodents, bats and non- human primates. Surveillance gap Hantaviruses pose a bigger systematic dan­ ger to Africa’s public health architecture than previously thought, argued de Oliveira and colleagues in a recent article. Limited diag­ nostic and testing capacity and lack of moni­ toring infrastructure, combined with climate change and urbanization, are leading to more zoonotic outbreaks. Africa has a clinical surveillance gap, with viral spillovers probably occurring without being detected by stretched public health authorities. During the current Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda, many of the early infections were suspected to be cases of malaria, leading to delays in the public health response. The DRC has the second highest bur­ den of malaria in the world, leading to tens of thousands of deaths each year. Many other zoonotic infections could be missed. Hillary Young, an ecologist at the University of California Santa Barbara, USA, notes that “we don’t know how big the burden of hanta­ virus is because we haven’t looked for it, really. We don’t have that surveillance.” “One of the acute problems facing Africa is that there is little clinical research into the ecology of hantaviruses, [such as] which specific animals host them,” she says. Such research, including genetics, would “empower scientists to map the interaction between hosts and viruses and calculate the possible harm to humans — in real time,” she adds. With surveillance capacity absent, doctors often report possible hantavirus infections as ‘fever of unknown origin’. “It’s hard, because hantavirus is another one of these diseases that kind of overlaps with lots of other unex­ plained febrile diseases,” says Young. This challenge persists despite South Africa having amongst the best infectious disease genomic surveillance infrastructure in the world. Laboratories across Africa are usually focused on supporting clinical studies in humans, but during outbreaks, resources are diverted to test animals for zoonotic infec­ tions. There are only a small number of such labs across the continent, such as the South Africa National Institute for Communicable Diseases, the Institut Pasteur de Dakar in Senegal and the Uganda Virus Research Unit. These labs act very quickly to develop reagents for new pathogens, test samples and develop metagenomics assays, but the bottleneck leads to inevitable delays, with zoonotic out­ breaks often underdiagnosed for weeks. Urbanization and deforestation Hantavirus spillover in Africa is likely to be linked to loss of biodiversity, rapid urbaniza­ tion and climate change. A recent outbreak of hantaviruses in South America spread beyond rural settings and into urban environments, Hantavirus particles under an electron microscope, with colour enhanced. CREDIT: ALFRED PASIEKA/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/GETTY nature health News possibly because climate variations are lead­ ing to milder and shorter winters in Argentina. Rapid urbanization — widespread across the continent — leads to increased risk, as rats breed in cities where residents regularly interact with wildlife. “We’ll have a bigger pro­ liferation of concentrated rodents,” in Africa’s fast-urbanizing landscapes, says Young, lead­ ing to more zoonotic outbreaks. Young’s research has shown how declines in large wildlife in East Africa were associated with an increase in the prevalence of a rodent- borne bacterium, Bartonella, which can infect humans — providing a link between biodiver­ sity loss and zoonotic disease outbreaks2. Climate change and change of land use in Africa drive rodents to find new breeding zones in human landscapes, warns Young. Rapid expansion of cities across Africa, many without investment in sewerage, creates food and opportunities for rodent species that are already adapted to live alongside humans. This creates the conditions for ‘boom dynamics’, says Young, where rodent popula­ tions increase rapidly. This means periods of explosive, exponential growth for rat popula­ tions followed by often calamitous declines3. “You might get really desperate rodents,” she says, where the animals are “forced into kind of aggressive behaviour. Fighting in rodents can help spread disease among them at higher prevalence.” One Health The genomic surveillance labs in Africa, Latin America and Asia have considerable expertise but fewer resources than their counterparts in high-income countries, says Young. Despite these constraints, they are doing valuable work closest to the regions where zoonotic diseases are most likely to spring up. Africa is taking a lead in shifting the ‘One Health’ model towards building long-term skills, surveillance and diagnostics infrastructure in the global south, the type of capacity that remains resilient through crises. Several African countries, including the DRC and Uganda, have adopted ‘One Health’ frame­ works, an approach pioneered by Rwanda4. But such frameworks need to extend beyond the countryside and integrate with cities in Africa, rather than thinking of these urban spaces as separated from wild rural environ­ ments, says Young. De Oliveira stresses that, although hanta­ viruses are unlikely to cause large human outbreaks — because of the biology of the virus — funding cuts for global health pose challenges. There is now a “big lack of global health funding,” he says, with the US and many Euro­ pean countries “running out of money for global health because of other priorities such as defence”. USA https://doi.org/ 10.1073/pnas.1404958111 (2014). 3. Doebeli, M., Jaque, E. C. & Ispolatov, Y. Commun. Biol. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-021-02021-4 (2021). 4. Henley, P. & Shyaka, A. Nat. analysis.background: Hantavirus infection risk in Africa is rising as rapid urbanization, deforestation and climate change alter rodent ecology, creating surveillance gaps that may leave many zoonotic events undetected (F1, F22).
analysis.methods: not reported in the supplied evidence
analysis.results: Experts state that hantavirus is likely more prevalent and widespread than diagnosed in Africa (F4) and that limited diagnostic capacity combined with climate change and urbanization is driving more spillover events (F8). Lethal Sangassou virus and other local strains circulate undetected in rodents, shrews and bats (F3). Transmission is mainly self‑limited clusters among rodents, other animals and humans (F5). Rapid urban growth promotes ‘boom dynamics’ of rodent populations, producing “desperate rodents” that may increase virus spread (F26).

papers.full_text: L’infection à hantavirus est une maladie à déclaration obligatoire au CanadaEn moyenne, 4 ou 5 cas d’infection à hantavirus sont confirmés chaque année au Canada. Dans presque tous les cas, la maladie est contractée en milieu agricole au Manitoba, en Saskatchewan, en Alberta et en Colombie-Britannique1. La transmission s’effectue généralement par contact avec des rongeurs infectés ou leurs excréments. Toutefois, l’espèce des Andes se distingue par sa capacité à être transmise entre personnes, généralement à la suite de contacts étroits et prolongés2. Les hantavirus causent 2 syndromes cliniquesLes espèces endémiques aux Amériques, y compris le virus des Andes, causent le syndrome cardiopulmonaire à hantavirus (SCPH), alors que les espèces européennes et asiatiques entraînent une fièvre hémorragique avec syndrome rénal (FHSR). Dans les 2 cas, la maladie se manifeste généralement après une incubation de 2 à 4 semaines, la médiane étant de 18 jours pour l’espèce des Andes. Le SCPH et la FHSR se manifestent d’abord par de la fièvre, des céphalées, une myalgie et des douleurs abdominales. Par la suite, le SCPH évolue vers un œdème pulmonaire, une insuffisance respiratoire, puis un choc cardiogénique, avec un taux de létalité de 12 % à 45 %. En revanche, la FHSR se caractérise par une insuffisance rénale aiguë et des manifestations hémorragiques (p. ex., épistaxis, hématurie, saignements gastro-intestinaux), avec un taux de létalité de 1 % à 12 %2,3. La sérologie et le test par amplification en chaîne par polymérase (ACP) s’effectuent au Laboratoire national de microbiologieLa présence d’anticorps de type immunoglobuline (Ig) M, une multiplication par au moins 4 du titre d’IgG ou la détection d’un hantavirus dans des échantillons sanguins analysés par ACP confirme l’infection à hantavirus. Le dépistage sérologique demeure la méthode diagnostique de préférence, alors que l’ACP est généralement utile dans la phase aiguë de l’infection1. On doit procéder à ces méthodes de dépistage sous la gouverne d’un ou d’une microbiologiste. Le traitement repose sur des mesures de soutienIl n’existe aucun vaccin ou traitement antiviral contre l’infection à hantavirus. Des études menées sur des animaux permettent de croire qu’on pourrait utiliser la ribavirine et le favipiravir tant pour le traitement que pour la prophylaxie postexposition4,5. On doit transférer les personnes chez qui on soupçonne un SCPH dans un établissement hospitalier doté de dispositifs d’oxygénation par membrane extracorporelle. Il est essentiel d’adopter des mesures préventives et de lutte contre les infections en cas de soupçon d’infection par le virus des AndesOn doit isoler toutes les personnes chez qui une infection par le virus des Andes est soupçonnée ou confirmée et prendre toutes les précautions contre la transmission par voie aérienne, par gouttelettes et par contact. Il faut également obtenir une consultation en infectiologie et aviser les autorités de santé publique locales6.Le JAMC vous invite à soumettre vos textes pour la rubrique « Cinq choses à savoir... » en ligne à https://mc.manuscriptcentral.com/cmaj.
